lessons.title: Personal Hygiene and Safe Handling of Herbal Materials
lessons.body:
When you handle medicinal plants, you are dealing with substances that can heal or harm. Your hands, clothes, and tools can carry dirt, bacteria, and even toxic plant residues. Always start by washing your hands with clean water and soap for at least 20 seconds before touching any plant material. If you are harvesting, wear clean glovesâespecially if you have cuts or scratches. For example, when harvesting Artemisia annua (used for malaria), wear gloves to avoid skin irritation from the plant's oils. Tie back long hair and avoid loose clothing that can catch on branches.

After harvesting, do not eat, drink, or smoke until you have washed your hands and face. Many herbs like neem or tobacco can leave residues that cause nausea if ingested accidentally. Use a dedicated apron or overalls for farm work, and wash them separately from family laundry with hot water and detergent. If you are handling dried herbs, wear a dust mask to avoid inhaling fine particles that can irritate your lungsâespecially with plants like pyrethrum or chili peppers.

Store harvested materials in clean, food-grade containers. Never use old pesticide bags or fuel containers. For fresh herbs, use clean baskets or crates that have been washed and sun-dried. If you are processing herbs for sale, keep a separate set of tools (knives, cutting boards) that are only used for herbal materials. Clean these tools with hot water and food-safe sanitizer after each use. A simple bleach solution (1 tablespoon of bleach per 1 gallon of water) can be used to sanitize surfaces, but rinse thoroughly with clean water afterwards.

Personal hygiene also means staying healthy yourself. Get enough rest, drink clean water, and eat well. If you are sick, especially with diarrhea or vomiting, do not handle herbs for sale or for medicine. You can spread germs. Train your workers or family members on these rules. Post a simple handwashing station near your drying and processing area: a jerrycan with a tap, soap, and a clean towel. This small investment prevents contamination and protects your business reputation.

lessons.title: Understanding Toxicity and Safe Dosages of Common Herbs
lessons.body:
Many herbs are safe when used correctly, but some can be poisonous if you take too much or use the wrong part. For example, the leaves of cassia (Senna) are a strong laxative; taking more than 1-2 grams of dried leaf can cause severe diarrhea and dehydration. The roots of comfrey contain alkaloids that can damage the liver if used internally for more than a few weeks. Always research the specific herb you are working with. A good rule: if you don't know the safe dose, start with a very small amount and never exceed the traditional use.

Dosages are usually given for dried herb. For most mild herbs like chamomile or peppermint, a safe tea is 1-2 teaspoons of dried herb per cup of boiling water, steeped for 5-10 minutes, up to 3 times a day. For stronger herbs like ginger, 1-2 grams of dried powder per day is typical. For bitter herbs like wormwood, do not exceed 1 gram per day, and do not use for more than 4 weeks. For children, use half or less of the adult dose, and consult a health worker. Pregnant women should avoid many herbs, including aloe vera latex, parsley, and mugwort, as they can cause miscarriage.

Toxicity can also come from contamination. Herbs grown near roadsides may contain lead from car exhaust. Herbs dried on bare ground can pick up animal waste. Always wash fresh herbs in clean water, and dry them on raised screens or clean mats. If you are selling herbs, label them with the recommended dose and warnings. For example, âDo not use if pregnant. Not for children under 12. Maximum 2 cups per day.â

If someone shows signs of poisoningâvomiting, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, or confusion after taking an herbâstop giving the herb immediately. Give them activated charcoal if available (1 gram per kilogram of body weight, mixed with water) and seek medical help. Keep a record of what herb was taken, how much, and when. This information helps doctors treat the patient. Never assume a natural product is automatically safe. Test small amounts on yourself before selling to others, and always err on the side of caution.

lessons.title: Avoiding Contamination: Clean Water, Tools, and Storage
lessons.body:
Contamination can ruin your herbal products and make people sick. The three biggest sources are dirty water, dirty tools, and poor storage. Start with water. Never use untreated river or well water for washing herbs or making tinctures. Boil water for 5 minutes, or use a filter with a 0.2-micron rating, or add 2 drops of household bleach (5% sodium hypochlorite) per liter of water and let it sit for 30 minutes. For rinsing herbs, use clean, cool boiled water. If you are making alcohol tinctures, use at least 40% alcohol (vodka or food-grade ethanol) to kill bacteria.

Tools must be cleaned before and after each use. Knives, cutting boards, mortars, and drying racks should be washed with hot soapy water, then rinsed with clean water, then sanitized with a bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per gallon of water). Let them air dry in the sun. Do not use wooden tools that have cracksâthey harbor bacteria. Use stainless steel or food-grade plastic. For drying, use clean cotton sheets or mesh screens. Never dry herbs on the ground, on old newspapers, or on surfaces treated with pesticides.

Storage is critical. Dried herbs absorb moisture and can grow mold, which produces aflatoxinsâpoisons that can cause liver cancer. Store dried herbs in airtight glass jars or food-grade plastic containers with tight lids. Keep them in a cool, dark, dry place. A simple test: if a dried leaf crumbles easily and snaps, it is dry enough. If it bends, it needs more drying. Add a small packet of silica gel (available in shoe boxes) to each jar to absorb moisture. Label each container with the herb name, date of harvest, and batch number. Use within 12 months for most dried herbs; 6 months for powdered herbs.

For fresh herbs, store in a refrigerator at 4Â°C (39Â°F) in perforated plastic bags for up to 1 week. For long-term storage, freeze in airtight bags. Never store herbs near chemicals, fuel, or strong-smelling items like onions or garlicâthey absorb odors. Clean your storage area monthly. Check for insects, rodents, or moisture. If you see mold, throw the whole batch away. Do not try to salvage it.

lessons.title: Meeting Local and Export Quality Standards
lessons.body:
If you want to sell your herbs locally or export them, you must meet quality standards. Locally, many African countries have national bureaus of standards (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, SON in Nigeria, SABS in South Africa). They set limits for moisture, ash, microbial contamination, and pesticide residues. For example, dried herbs for export to the EU must have less than 10% moisture, less than 10% total ash, and no more than 10^4 CFU/g of total bacteria. They also test for heavy metals like lead (max 5 mg/kg) and cadmium (max 1 mg/kg).

To meet these standards, you need good agricultural and collection practices (GACP). That means: record everythingâwhen you planted, what you sprayed, when you harvested, how you dried. Use only approved pesticides, and stop spraying at least 2 weeks before harvest. Harvest at the right time: for leaves, before flowering; for roots, after the plant dies back. Dry quickly in a solar dryer or well-ventilated shed at 40-50Â°C. Do not dry in direct sun if the herb contains volatile oils (like mint or basil)âit reduces quality.

After drying, clean the herbs by removing foreign matter: stones, dirt, other plants. Sieve or winnow. Then grade by size and color. Package in clean, new bags or boxes. For export, you often need a certificate of analysis (COA) from a lab. Find a local lab that tests for moisture, ash, microbes, and pesticides. A basic test can cost $50-$200. It is worth it because buyers will reject shipments without a COA.

Also, follow fair labor practices. Many export markets require that no child labor was used and that workers were paid fairly. Keep simple records of who worked and how much they were paid. If you are organic, get certified by a local organic body (e.g., ECOCERT in West Africa). Certification takes 2-3 years and costs money, but it can double your price. Start small: sell to local health shops and pharmacies first. Ask them what standards they need. Then gradually improve your practices to meet export requirements. Join a cooperativeâit is cheaper to get testing and certification as a group.

lessons.title: Labeling Requirements for Herbal Products
lessons.body:
A good label protects you and your customers. In most African countries, herbal products sold as medicine must be registered with the national drug authority (e.g., NAFDAC in Nigeria, SAHPRA in South Africa, PPB in Kenya). For simple herbal teas or cosmetics, rules are lighter, but you still need clear labels. At minimum, your label must include: product name, net weight, list of ingredients (common and scientific names), part of plant used, batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date, and your contact details (name, address, phone).

If you make a health claimâlike âhelps with digestionâ or ârelieves coughââyou may need to prove it. In many countries, you cannot claim to cure or treat a disease without drug registration. For example, saying âcures malariaâ is illegal for an unregistered product. Instead, use traditional use statements: âTraditionally used to support digestion.â Always add a disclaimer: âThis statement has not been evaluated by the drug authority. Not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.â

Include warnings and dosage. For example: âAdults: 1 cup of tea, 2-3 times daily. Do not exceed 3 cups per day. Not for children under 12. Do not use if pregnant or breastfeeding. Consult a health worker if symptoms persist.â If your product contains alcohol, state the percentage. If it contains honey, state that it is not for infants under 1 year. For external use only, write that clearly.

Use waterproof labels that won't smudge. Print in the official language of your country, and if you export, add English, French, or Portuguese as needed. Keep a copy of every label you use. If you sell online, include the same information on your website. For small batches, you can print labels at a local print shop for about $0.10 per label. For larger runs, use a professional printer. Never use handwritten labels for products you sellâthey look unprofessional and can be rejected by buyers. A clean, informative label builds trust and helps you stand out.

lessons.title: First Aid for Common Farming Injuries
lessons.body:
Farming herbs can cause cuts, sprains, insect stings, and heat exhaustion. Be prepared. Keep a first aid kit in your shed or vehicle. It should contain: clean water, soap, antiseptic cream, sterile gauze, adhesive bandages, elastic bandage, scissors, tweezers, disposable gloves, a thermometer, oral rehydration salts (ORS), and a first aid manual. Check it every 3 months and replace expired items.

For cuts and scrapes: wash your hands, put on gloves, then rinse the wound with clean water for 5 minutes. Apply pressure with gauze to stop bleeding. Apply antiseptic and cover with a sterile bandage. If the cut is deep, gaping, or won't stop bleeding after 10 minutes, go to a clinic. If you cut yourself on a tool that was used on toxic plants, wash the wound with soap and water immediately, and seek medical adviceâsome plant toxins can enter through cuts.

For sprains and strains: use the RICE methodâRest, Ice (or cold water), Compression, Elevation. Wrap an elastic bandage snugly but not too tight. If you feel numbness or tingling, loosen it. For insect stings or snake bites: remove the stinger if present, wash the area, apply a cold pack. For snake bites, keep the person calm and still, immobilize the bitten limb, and get to a hospital immediately. Do not cut the wound or suck out venom. For scorpion stings, apply a cold pack and seek medical help if symptoms like difficulty breathing occur.

Heat exhaustion: move to shade, loosen clothing, give cool water with ORS, and fan the person. If they are confused or unconscious, it is heat strokeâa medical emergency. Call for help and cool them rapidly with wet cloths. For chemical exposure (e.g., pesticides): remove contaminated clothing, wash skin with soap and water for 15 minutes, and flush eyes with clean water for 15 minutes. If swallowed, do not induce vomiting unless told by a poison control center. Keep the pesticide label with you for the doctor. Always work with a partner when using dangerous tools or chemicals. Never work alone in remote fields. Know the emergency number for your local clinic or ambulance. A simple phone tree with neighbors can save a life.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Health, Safety, and Quality Standards for Medicinal & Herbal Plant Cultivation

Module: Health, Safety, and Quality Standards  |  Lesson: Practical Reference  |  Level: Rise AFRICA Skills

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into a single working document you can keep at the farm, the drying shed, or the processing room. For an African agribusiness, health and safety is not only a legal obligation â it is a market-access tool. Buyers in Europe, North America, and the Gulf increasingly require documented hygiene, traceability, and residue control before they will sign a supply contract. A farmer who cannot show clean water records, calibrated drying, and correct labelling will lose that contract to a competitor who can.

Treat the standards below as a business system: every control you put in place reduces rejection risk, protects your brand, and raises the price your herbal material can command.

1. Personal Hygiene and Safe Handling of Herbal Materials

Herbal materials are consumed or applied to the body, so they must be treated like food or medicine â never like ordinary agricultural produce. The human body is the single largest contamination source on most smallholder farms.

  • Hands: Wash with soap and clean running water before handling, after using the toilet, after handling waste, and after touching animals. Dry with a clean cloth or air-dry.
  • Clothing: Wear clean, washable work clothing. Avoid loose jewellery, watches, and rings that trap soil and microbes.
  • Illness: Workers with diarrhoea, vomiting, open wounds, or skin infections must not handle herbal material until cleared.
  • Harvesting: Use clean, dedicated harvest knives and baskets. Never place harvested herbs directly on bare ground â use clean tarpaulins or crates.
  • Separation: Keep harvested herbs away from livestock, poultry, and household waste at all times.

2. Understanding Toxicity and Safe Dosages of Common Herbs

Many African medicinal plants are pharmacologically active and can be toxic at the wrong dose, the wrong plant part, or the wrong preparation. Growers and processors must know the difference between a safe traditional preparation and a hazardous one.

Table 1: Toxicity and safe-use notes for selected African medicinal plants
Plant Part used Key safety concern Practical control
Artemisia afra (African wormwood) Leaf Essential oils (thujone) can cause nausea, seizures at high doses; not for infants or pregnancy Limit to traditional infusion doses; label clearly "not for children under 12 or pregnant women"
Aloe ferox / Aloe vera Leaf gel / latex Latex (aloin) is a strong laxative; prolonged internal use causes electrolyte loss Separate gel from latex; restrict latex products to short-term use only
Moringa oleifera Leaf, seed, root Root and bark contain alkaloids; seed pods may affect fertility; leaf is generally safe Market leaf powder as food/nutrition; do not sell root as a general tonic
Sutherlandia frutescens (Cancer bush) Leaf, seed May interact with antiretrovirals and immunosuppressants Add interaction warning on label; advise consulting a clinician
Pelargonium sidoides (Umckaloabo) Root Rare liver and bleeding concerns; not for pregnancy Standardised extracts only; avoid unregulated high-dose root powders

Source: World Health Organization, WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Vols. 1â4 (WHO, Geneva); and van Wyk, B-E., Wink, M., Medicinal Plants of the World (CABI).

3. Avoiding Contamination: Clean Water, Tools, and Storage

Contamination is the leading cause of rejected herbal consignments from Africa. It usually comes from three sources: water, tools, and storage.

Water

Irrigation and washing water must meet microbiological and chemical limits. Test borehole or river water at least once per season for E. coli, nitrates, and heavy metals. Where testing is unavailable, use potable or treated water for final washing and processing.

Tools and equipment

Use food-grade stainless steel, plastic, or clean wood. Clean and sanitise knives, drying trays, and mills between batches. Never use the same equipment for manure, agrochemicals, and herbal material.

Drying and storage

Dry herbs to a moisture content of 8â12% (leaves and flowers) or 10â14% (roots and bark) to prevent mould and aflatoxin formation. Store in clean, dry, pest-proof containers away from sunlight, fuels, and pesticides. Keep a batch record of date, weight, moisture, and operator.

4. Meeting Local and Export Quality Standards

African growers must meet two layers of standards: national regulations (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria, SAHPRA in South Africa, Ghana Standards Authority) and destination-market rules (EU pharmacopoeia, US FDA, Gulf standards). The most common export requirements are:

  • Maximum pesticide residue limits (MRLs) â often at or near the limit of detection.
  • Heavy metal limits: lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury.
  • Microbiological limits: total aerobic count, E. coli, Salmonella, moulds, yeasts.
  • Aflatoxin limits (especially for roots, bark, and stored powders).
  • Identification and purity â correct botanical species, no adulteration.
  • Documentation: certificate of analysis, phytosanitary certificate, GACP/GMP evidence, and traceability records.
Table 2: Typical quality parameters and indicative limits for dried herbal material
Parameter Indicative limit Why it matters Source
Moisture content 8â12% (leaf/flower); 10â14% (root/bark) Prevents mould and aflatoxin WHO GACP (2003)
Total ash Typically â¤ 10â15% Indicates soil/foreign matter WHO monographs
Lead (Pb) â¤ 5 mg/kg (many markets â¤ 3 mg/kg) Heavy metal toxicity EU/WHO limits
Cadmium (Cd) â¤ 1 mg/kg Accumulates in roots EU/WHO limits
Aflatoxins (total) â¤ 4â10 Âµg/kg Liver toxicity, carcinogenic Codex Alimentarius
E. coli Absent in 1 g Faecal contamination WHO/Codex
Salmonella Absent in 10 g Food safety WHO/Codex

Sources: WHO Guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP) for Medicinal Plants (2003); Codex Alimentarius General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995); European Pharmacopoeia general monographs.

5. Labelling Requirements for Herbal Products

Correct labelling is a legal requirement and a marketing asset. At minimum, every package should carry:

  • Product name and botanical name (genus and species).
  • Plant part used (leaf, root, bark, seed).
  • Net weight or volume.
  • Batch or lot number and date of manufacture/expiry.
  • Name and physical address of the producer or packer.
  • Country of origin.
  • Directions for use and recommended dose.
  • Safety warnings (e.g., "not for use in pregnancy", "consult a health professional").
  • Storage conditions.
  • For exports: barcode, country of destination language, and any required regulatory number.

â  SAFETY WARNING â TOXIC PLANTS AND DOSAGE

Never sell or distribute a herbal product without a known botanical identity, a safe dose, and a clear label. Some African medicinal plants (e.g., Artemisia afra, Aloe latex, Sutherlandia frutescens) can cause serious harm â including seizures, liver damage, bleeding, or dangerous drug interactions â at high doses or in pregnancy. Do not recommend herbal treatment for infants, pregnant women, or people on prescription medicines without qualified clinical advice. Keep all treated seed, agrochemicals, and toxic plant material locked away from food, children, and livestock. If poisoning is suspected, contact your nearest poison centre or hospital immediately and bring the plant or product label with you.

6. First Aid for Common Farming Injuries

Farm injuries are common and often preventable. Keep a stocked first-aid kit in the shed and train at least two workers in basic response.

  • Cuts and machete wounds: Apply direct pressure with a clean dressing, elevate, and seek medical care if bleeding does not stop or the wound is deep.
  • Snakebite: Keep the victim calm and still, immobilise the limb below heart level, remove tight items, and transport to hospital immediately. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet.
  • Insect stings and bites: Remove the sting, apply a cold compress, and watch for signs of anaphylaxis (swelling of face/throat, difficulty breathing) â this is a medical emergency.
  • Chemical exposure: Move to fresh air, remove contaminated clothing, wash skin with plenty of water, and take the product label to the clinic.
  • Heat exhaustion: Move to shade, give oral rehydration solution, and cool the body with wet cloths.
  • Eye injuries: Flush with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Clean water tested and potable water used for final washing.
  2. Hands washed and clean clothing worn before handling herbs.
  3. No sick workers handling herbal material.
  4. Tools cleaned and sanitised between batches; no shared use with agrochemicals.
  5. Herbs dried to correct moisture (8â12% leaf, 10â14% root) and stored pest-proof.
  6. Batch records kept: date, weight, moisture, operator, lot number.
  7. Labels complete: botanical name, plant part, dose, warnings, batch, origin.
  8. First-aid kit stocked and at least two workers trained.
  9. Toxic plants and chemicals locked away from food and children.

Further Reading

  • WHO Guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP) for Medicinal Plants â World Health Organization, free PDF.
  • FAO: Quality Control of Herbal Medicines and Related Areas â Food and Agriculture Organization.
  • Codex Alimentarius â General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995).
  • European Medicines Agency â Herbal Product Guidelines.
  • WHO African Region â Traditional Medicine Resources.

Business takeaway: Every hygiene, toxicity, contamination, quality, labelling, and first-aid control you implement is a direct investment in your ability to sell at a premium, win export contracts, and build a trusted African herbal brand.

quiz.q: What is the minimum time you should wash your hands with soap and water before handling herbal materials?
quiz.explanation: 20 seconds is the recommended time to effectively remove germs and residues.

quiz.q: Which of the following should you wear when harvesting Artemisia annua to avoid skin irritation?
quiz.explanation: Artemisia annua oils can irritate skin, so gloves and long sleeves protect you.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid eating or smoking after handling herbs before washing?
options: B) Residues can cause nausea if ingested
D) It makes herbs less potent
quiz.explanation: Plant residues on hands can be accidentally ingested and cause illness.

quiz.q: What is a safe sanitizing solution for tools used with herbal materials?
options: A) 1 tablespoon bleach per gallon of water
B) 1 cup bleach per gallon of water
quiz.explanation: A diluted bleach solution is effective and safe when rinsed thoroughly.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign that you should NOT handle herbs for sale?
options: B) You have diarrhea or vomiting
D) You have a slight cough
quiz.explanation: Diarrhea and vomiting can spread germs to the herbs, contaminating them.

quiz.q: What is a safe daily dose of dried ginger powder for most adults?
quiz.explanation: 1-2 grams per day is a typical safe dose for ginger.

quiz.q: Which herb should pregnant women avoid because it can cause miscarriage?
quiz.explanation: Aloe vera latex is a strong laxative and can stimulate the uterus.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended daily dose of dried wormwood?
quiz.explanation: Wormwood is potent; exceeding 1 gram per day can cause toxicity.

quiz.q: If someone shows signs of herb poisoning, what should you give them if available?
quiz.explanation: Activated charcoal binds to toxins and can reduce absorption.

quiz.q: Why should you not dry herbs on bare ground?
options: B) They can pick up animal waste and dirt
quiz.explanation: Ground drying exposes herbs to contamination from soil, animals, and microbes.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of alcohol for making tinctures to kill bacteria?
quiz.explanation: At least 40% alcohol is needed to effectively kill bacteria and preserve tinctures.

quiz.q: How should you test if a dried herb is dry enough for storage?
quiz.explanation: Crumbling and snapping indicates low moisture, which prevents mold.

quiz.q: What is a danger of storing herbs with onions or garlic?
quiz.explanation: Herbs can absorb strong odors from onions and garlic, ruining their quality.

quiz.q: What is the maximum moisture content for dried herbs exported to the EU?
quiz.explanation: EU standards typically require less than 10% moisture to prevent microbial growth.

quiz.q: What does GACP stand for?
options: A) Good Agricultural and Collection Practices
quiz.explanation: GACP is the international standard for producing quality herbal materials.

quiz.q: When should you stop spraying pesticides before harvest?
quiz.explanation: A 2-week pre-harvest interval allows pesticide residues to degrade to safe levels.

quiz.q: What is a Certificate of Analysis (COA)?
options: A) A label for your product
B) A lab report showing quality test results
quiz.explanation: A COA from a lab confirms that your herbs meet specified quality standards.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of workers and wages for export?
options: B) To prove fair labor practices
D) To sell to local markets
quiz.explanation: Many export markets require proof that no child labor was used and workers were paid fairly.

quiz.q: What is the minimum information required on a herbal product label?
options: B) Product name, ingredients, batch number, expiry date, contact
D) A picture of the plant
quiz.explanation: These details ensure traceability and safety for consumers.

quiz.q: Which claim is illegal for an unregistered herbal product in most countries?
quiz.explanation: Claiming to cure a disease requires drug registration; unregistered products cannot make such claims.

quiz.q: What should you include on a label if your product contains honey?
quiz.explanation: Honey can contain botulism spores, which are dangerous for infants under 1 year.

quiz.q: What is the recommended first aid for a minor cut?
options: B) Wash with clean water, apply antiseptic, cover
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and covering prevents infection.

quiz.q: What does the RICE method stand for in treating sprains?
quiz.explanation: RICE reduces swelling and pain for sprains and strains.

quiz.q: What should you do for a snake bite?
options: A) Cut the wound and suck out venom
B) Keep the person calm and still, immobilize limb, seek help
quiz.explanation: Cutting or sucking is dangerous; immobilization and rapid medical care are key.

quiz.q: What is the first step for chemical exposure on the skin?
options: B) Remove contaminated clothing and wash with soap and water
quiz.explanation: Removing contaminated clothing and washing prevents further absorption.

quiz.q: Why should you work with a partner when using dangerous tools or chemicals?
options: B) To have someone to call for help in an emergency
quiz.explanation: A partner can provide first aid or call for help if an accident occurs.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to dry herbs to preserve volatile oils?
options: B) Solar dryer or well-ventilated shed at 40-50Â°C
quiz.explanation: Moderate heat and good airflow preserve oils better than high heat or direct sun.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mold on stored dried herbs?
options: A) Scrape it off and use
B) Throw the whole batch away
quiz.explanation: Mold can produce aflatoxins that are invisible and dangerous; discard the entire batch.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a batch number on a label?
options: A) To track the product in case of problems
B) To make it look professional
quiz.explanation: Batch numbers allow traceability if a product needs to be recalled.

quiz.q: How often should you check your first aid kit?
quiz.explanation: Regular checks ensure supplies are stocked and not expired.
